To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a series of DIPs were designed and synthesized with large structural diversity, their DNA binding properties were studied by UV‐Vis titration, and their biological activities were determined by tetra zolium dye‐ based microtitration assays.
we have synthesised a large library of DIP compounds that can bind to DNA with a range of binding constants, intercalate into DNA, and have cytotoxic activity.
we have synthesised a large number of dihydroimidazo-phenanthridinium cation (DIPs), with a wide range of structural diversity, and determined their DNA binding constants and cytotoxicity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis and characterisation of a library of dihyroimidazophenathridinium (DIPS) with large structural variation.
the synthesis and biological evaluation of dihydroimidazo[4′,5′:1,2]phenanthridinium salts.
the design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of a new family of dihydroimidazo‐phenanthridinium cationic compounds, which we have named dihydroimidazopheanthridinium (or DIP) compounds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DIPs are a class of DNA binding agents that are capable of interacting with DNA by inter‐ or minor‐groove‐binding and that can be tuned to have a range of biological activities.
the DIPs are a class of molecules with potential as DNA binding agents, and that the results provide a basis for future design of DNA binding agents with tuneable structures.
the DNA binding properties of DIP cations are dependent upon their structures and that the cytotoxic activities of DIPs are dependent on their DNA binding properties.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the DNA‐binding properties of the dihydroimidazopyridinium (DHP) cation can be modified by introducing an aromatic substituent on the pyridinium nitrogen atom, and the resulting compounds can be designed to interact with DNA by both intercalation and minor‐groove recognition.
we have shown how the DNA binding and cytotoxic properties of a series of DIP cations can be controlled by the nature and number of substituents on the DIP core.
we have developed a “one‐ pot” method for the synthesis of a library of DIP cations, which have a wide range of structures and DNA binding properties.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the DIPs have the potential to be developed as anticancer agents, and the results provide a basis for further work in this area.
the DIP cations can bind to DNA in an intercalation‐like manner.
DIPs with tuneable structures can be synthesised and that these DIPs have the potential to be used as DNA binding agents.
